title: Photography and Hyper-Realism
answer: Synthetic portraiture, lighting rigs, upscaling, product mockups and virtual location scouting.

children.name: Synthetic Portraiture
children.blurb: Synthetic portraiture is the making of human or human-like likenesses with generative image models, whether the subject is a real person, a composite, or a wholly invented face.

children.name: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
children.blurb: Lighting rigs and relighting cover the setup and control of light in a photograph or a rendered image, and the later adjustment of that light after the fact.

children.name: Upscaling and Noise Reduction
children.blurb: Upscaling and noise reduction cover the post processing steps that take a finished or nearly finished image and make it larger, cleaner, or both.

children.name: Product and Fashion Mockups
children.blurb: Product and fashion mockups cover the generated or composited imagery that stands in for a photograph of an object or garment before the real shoot happens.

children.name: Virtual Location Scouting
children.blurb: Virtual location scouting is the practice of finding, generating, or assembling a plausible place for a shoot before anyone travels there.

sections.body: This section covers the use of generative image models to produce photographs that were never taken, or to repair and extend photographs that were. In practice, synthetic portraiture is used for headshots, character design and stock imagery, where a model is prompted or fine tuned on a face and returns a plausible person at a chosen age, expression and framing. Lighting rigs and relighting tools let a user move a light source after the fact, changing the direction, colour and softness of illumination on an existing subject. Upscaling and noise reduction take a low resolution or grainy frame and reconstruct detail that was not captured, which is now routine in restoration, print preparation and phone photography. Product and fashion mockups place garments and objects into generated scenes so that a catalogue can be shot without a studio, and virtual location scouting generates or assembles backdrops before anyone travels to a real place.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The technical work is far enough along that a single generated portrait can pass casual inspection, and relighting and upscaling are reliable enough to sit inside ordinary editing pipelines. What is not solved is consistency: the same synthetic person drifts between images, hands and teeth still fail under scrutiny, and upscalers invent texture that looks like detail but is not evidence of anything. Provenance is the other open problem, since generated photographs carry no inherent record of their origin, and detection tools lag behind the generators they are meant to catch. The legal position is unsettled rather than resolved, and this site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a number that reflects how much of the field is still being argued over rather than settled. Anyone using these tools for commercial work, journalism or evidence faces real limits, and the honest summary is that the images look convincing long before the surrounding rules and verification methods do.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here divide the work by what part of the photographic pipeline they touch. Synthetic Portraiture is the entry point, covering how a face is generated, conditioned and kept stable across a set, and it is where most readers should start. Lighting Rigs and Relighting goes a level deeper into illumination, treating light as an editable variable rather than something fixed at capture, while Upscaling and Noise Reduction deals with the opposite end, recovering and enlarging what already exists. Product and Fashion Mockups applies both of those to commercial imagery, where the subject must stay accurate to a real object even as the scene around it is invented. Virtual Location Scouting closes the set by covering the backgrounds themselves, the places that are generated or assembled before a shoot, and it is the page to read when the question is where an image is supposed to be rather than who or what is in it.
